evidence.title: BUN (blood urea nitrogen) test
evidence.publisher: MedlinePlus · U.S. National Library of Medicine
aliases: การทำงานของไต
evidence.content: A BUN test measures urea nitrogen, a waste product made when the liver breaks down protein and removed from the blood by the kidneys. It is often ordered with creatinine, for example in a basic metabolic panel, to check kidney function. A high BUN can occur with kidney disease, dehydration, a high-protein diet, heart failure, bleeding in the digestive tract or some medicines; a low BUN is less common and may be seen with liver disease or malnutrition. A BUN-to-creatinine ratio is sometimes reported to help interpretation.

evidence.title: Chloride blood test
evidence.publisher: MedlinePlus · U.S. National Library of Medicine
aliases: อิเล็กโทรไลต์
evidence.content: Chloride is an electrolyte that works with sodium, potassium and bicarbonate to help control the body's fluid balance and acid-base balance. It is usually measured in an electrolyte panel or metabolic panel, and its level often changes in the same direction as sodium. Abnormal chloride levels can be linked to dehydration, prolonged vomiting or diarrhea, kidney problems, acid-base disturbances or some medicines. Chloride is interpreted with the other electrolytes rather than on its own.

evidence.title: Chronic kidney disease tests & diagnosis
evidence.publisher: NIDDK · U.S. National Institutes of Health
aliases: โรคไตเรื้อรัง

อัลบูมินในปัสสาวะ

evidence.content: NIDDK explains that early kidney disease usually has no symptoms, so blood and urine tests are the only way to know how the kidneys are working. A creatinine blood test is used to estimate the glomerular filtration rate (eGFR): an eGFR of 60 or more is in the normal range, below 60 may mean kidney disease, and 15 or less may mean kidney failure. A urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) below 30 mg/g is normal, while 30 mg/g or more may be a sign of kidney disease. Because results can change for temporary reasons, abnormal tests are repeated over about 3 months to confirm kidney disease.

evidence.title: Estimating glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
evidence.publisher: NIDDK · U.S. National Institutes of Health
aliases: อัตราการกรองของไต
การทำงานของไต
อีจีเอฟอาร์
evidence.content: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the best overall measure of kidney function, but it is rarely measured directly; instead it is estimated (eGFR) from serum creatinine using an equation that also uses age and sex. NIDDK recommends the 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation, which does not include a race term. eGFR is reported in mL/min/1.73 m² and is less accurate when creatinine is not stable or in people with very high or very low muscle mass, where adding cystatin C can improve the estimate. eGFR is read together with urine albumin and over time.

evidence.title: KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline: GFR and albuminuria categories
evidence.publisher: KDIGO · Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes
aliases: ระยะโรคไตเรื้อรัง
อัลบูมินในปัสสาวะ
evidence.content: KDIGO classifies CKD by cause, GFR category and albuminuria category. GFR categories in mL/min/1.73 m² are G1 90 or above, G2 60 to 89, G3a 45 to 59, G3b 30 to 44, G4 15 to 29 and G5 below 15 (kidney failure). Albuminuria categories by urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio are A1 below 30 mg/g, A2 30 to 300 mg/g and A3 above 300 mg/g. G1 and G2 count as CKD only when markers of kidney damage are present, and a category is assigned only after abnormalities have lasted more than 3 months.
